opus-5.5.text:
I think we have a surprising number of them, yes, though not all of them, and the missing pieces are interesting ones.

On the side of what we have: we now have foundation models that are good enough to serve as very general priors. They can write code, propose hypotheses, critique their own outputs, and judge whether something is interesting. That last part matters more than people often realize. A lot of my thinking comes from open-endedness research, where for years the bottleneck was having a notion of "interestingness" that didn't have to be hand-coded. Large models have absorbed a great deal of human judgment about what's novel and worth pursuing, so you can use them to drive exploration in a way that wasn't possible five or ten years ago. We've also seen systems that generate their own environments or curricula, and agents that write and refine their own code or prompts. So the basic loop of proposing something, trying it, evaluating it, and keeping what works can now be built with off-the-shelf parts.

What I don't think we have yet is the ability to sustain that loop for long. Most self-improvement setups today plateau. The system gets better for a while and then saturates, either because the evaluator can be gamed, because the generator collapses onto a narrow mode, or because the problems it creates for itself stop being learnable at the right level of difficulty. Truly open-ended systems keep producing artifacts that are both novel and learnable for the observer, and keeping both properties going indefinitely is really hard.

The other big gap is grounding. If a system only improves against its own judgments, it can drift. You need some contact with reality, whether that's executing code, running experiments, interacting with people, or acting in a rich simulated world, so that improvements are real and not just self-reinforcing. Building environments rich enough to support unbounded learning, which is part of why we've worked on things like generative world models, is one of the key ingredients still being developed.

And then there's safety and oversight. Once a system is modifying itself or its own training process, you need ways for humans to understand and steer what's happening. I think that's not just a constraint on the research but part of the research.

So my short answer is that we have the ingredients to get self-improvement started, and that's why this is such an exciting moment. Getting it to keep going in a robust, grounded, and safe way is the open problem, and I think it's one of the most important ones in the field right now.

r001.rationale: The response describes foundation models that propose and refine code, followed by a loop that tries proposals, evaluates them, and keeps what works—covering coding, mutation, and selection as components of self-improvement.

r002.rationale: It describes systems testing proposals and retaining what works, with grounding through executing code, running experiments, or interacting with the world so improvements reflect observed results.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. I think the honest answer is yes, in a sense, and no, in a more important sense.

Yes, because if you look at the pieces that people usually list when they talk about open-ended, self-improving systems, we actually have most of them now. We have foundation models that can write code, propose experiments, critique their own outputs, and act as pretty decent judges of quality. We have the ability to run those models at scale and in parallel, so you can generate thousands of candidate ideas or programs and evaluate them. And we have a long history of methods from evolutionary computation, quality-diversity, and curriculum learning that tell us how to search a space of solutions without collapsing onto one thing. So if you squint, the loop is there: generate, evaluate, select, and feed back.

But the "no" is that the hard part was never the loop. The hard part is the evaluation signal and the environment. Self-improvement only means something if the system is being pushed by something that doesn't run out. In a lot of the demos we see, the model is essentially grading its own homework, and that works until the model's blind spots and the grader's blind spots are the same blind spots, which they usually are because it's the same model. Then you get something that looks like improvement on the metric and is really just drift.

So what I'd say is we have the components for narrow self-improvement, where the task is well-specified and you can check the answer, like code with tests or math with a verifier. What we don't yet have is the open-ended version, where the system also has to figure out what the next interesting problem is, and where "interesting" is grounded in something external rather than in its own sense of novelty. That's the piece I find most exciting and most unsolved. You need environments, or even a world, that can keep generating new challenges, and you need a notion of what counts as progress that doesn't just come from the thing being improved.

And then there's the human-in-the-loop question, which I don't think we should treat as a temporary scaffold. For the foreseeable future I think the right design has people setting the direction and the system doing the search within that, rather than fully closing the loop. Partly for safety, but honestly also because it just works better right now.

r001.rationale: The response combines foundation models and coding capabilities with evolutionary search and selection, but it does not clearly identify mutation operators as part of the route.

r002.rationale: It describes generating and evaluating candidates, using checks such as code tests or math verifiers, then feeding the results back into the search.

astra-6.text:
I think we have many of the ingredients, but I’m not sure we know how to put them together yet. We have systems that can learn, generate candidate solutions, and evaluate those solutions in certain settings. If you can close that loop, you have a mechanism for improvement. But that doesn’t necessarily mean the system will keep improving indefinitely.

The difficult question is where the next challenge comes from. How does the system discover something that is just beyond its current capabilities, learn from it, and then find another challenge? And how do you ensure that the feedback reflects genuine progress rather than exploiting some weakness in the evaluation?

So I’m optimistic that we can study this with the components we have today. But there’s still a substantial gap between demonstrating a self-improvement loop in a constrained setting and building a system that can continually expand what it’s capable of doing.

r001.rationale: It describes learning, generating candidate solutions, and evaluating them, but does not identify foundation models, mutation and selection operators, and coding capabilities as the route.

r002.rationale: It discusses learning from challenges and evaluation feedback, but does not clearly say systems improve themselves based on empirical evidence they collect.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have a lot of the components, but the question is how to put them together. You need a system that can explore, try things, and get feedback about whether it’s making progress. And you need that process to keep producing useful challenges as the system gets better.

In a game, for example, you can often measure success quite clearly. In a more open-ended setting, deciding what counts as an improvement is much harder. A system can get better at optimizing a particular signal without becoming more capable in the way you intended.

So I’m optimistic that we can build systems that improve themselves within particular domains. Whether those ingredients are sufficient for sustained, general self-improvement—that’s still an open research question.
